issues.legal_issue: In an appeal available as of right after an acquittal is reversed and a conviction is entered, the Supreme Court must decide the case on its merits rather than limit review to whether the High Court had sufficient grounds to interfere with the acquittal.
material_facts: The accused were acquitted at trial and convicted by the High Court in the State’s appeal against acquittal.
The accused brought an appeal under the provision granting an appeal as of right in the specified circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court had to consider all questions of fact and law and decide the appeal on its merits; whether the High Court had sufficient grounds to reverse the acquittal was not material to that review.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(a) of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 provides the specified accused with an appeal as of right. In such an appeal the Supreme Court acts as an appellate court and decides questions of fact and law on the merits. The limits relevant to the Court’s discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, including principles governing a High Court’s interference with an acquittal, do not govern this statutory appeal. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.

predicates.statutory_criminal_appeal_as_of_right: The accused brought a criminal appeal that the law makes available as of right in the circumstances.
predicates.trial_acquittal_reversed: The trial court acquitted the accused, and a higher court reversed that acquittal.
predicates.high_court_conviction_entered: The High Court convicted the accused after the acquittal was reversed.

issues.definition: When an appeal as of right follows a reversed trial acquittal and a High Court conviction, the Supreme Court decides the appeal on its merits.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution evidence was sufficient to establish the accused’s participation in the assault beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: An injured eyewitness testified that the accused attacked the deceased and that she was injured during the occurrence.
Two other eyewitnesses testified that they came to the scene during the assault and saw the attack.
The injured eyewitness made a prompt report identifying the accused and describing their roles and weapons.
The eyewitnesses were found to be natural witnesses, and the injured eyewitness’s injuries supported her presence at the scene.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness testimony was acceptable, and the prosecution proved its case against the appellants beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the credibility of the eyewitnesses against their presence and injuries, the promptness and contents of the first report, and the surrounding evidence. It agreed with the High Court that the witnesses were natural and reliable. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this evidentiary conclusion.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_after_acquittal and injured_witness_present and prompt_report_supports_account and corroborating_eyewitnesses_present

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_acquittal: The accused challenged a conviction entered after an acquittal in a criminal appeal.
predicates.injured_witness_present: A witness who was injured in the occurrence testified to having witnessed it.
predicates.prompt_report_supports_account: An early report identified the accused and described the occurrence consistently with the witness’s account.
predicates.corroborating_eyewitnesses_present: Other eyewitnesses testified to seeing the assault and their testimony supported the injured witness’s account.

issues.definition: When an injured witness was present, an early report supports her account, and other eyewitnesses corroborate it in an appeal following acquittal, the prosecution case is proved beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of private defence of property fails when the defence does not provide material supporting its claimed possession and the evidence supports the opposing party’s possession and cultivation.
material_facts: The accused claimed that they were in possession of the field and that the deceased came to disturb that possession.
The accused produced neither an order vacating the interim arrangement concerning possession nor records showing that they had raised the crop.
Revenue extracts recorded the deceased as owner, cultivator, and the person who raised the crop.
The injured eyewitness’s evidence that the deceased and she had raised the crop was unrebutted.
Eight accused were harvesting the crop with weapons, while the deceased and his wife were the only opposing persons who came to the field.
issues.conclusion: The plea of private defence of property was negatived because the accused failed to establish the factual basis for it and the evidence supported the prosecution’s account of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 97, secondly, read with section 99 of the Indian Penal Code, the asserted right of private defence of property was considered on the material in the record, but the defence had the duty to make the necessary supporting material available. The Court assessed the claim against the possession and cultivation evidence and the surrounding circumstances. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: criminal_assault_case and private_defence_of_property_claimed and defence_lacks_possession_support and evidence_supports_other_party_possession

predicates.criminal_assault_case: The case concerns an assault arising from a dispute over possession of property.
predicates.private_defence_of_property_claimed: The accused asserted that they used force to protect their possession of property.
predicates.defence_lacks_possession_support: The accused did not produce material supporting their claimed possession or showing that the other party’s asserted entitlement to possession had ended.
predicates.evidence_supports_other_party_possession: Documents, testimony, or surrounding circumstances supported the other party’s possession and cultivation of the property.

issues.definition: In an assault case involving a claimed defence of property, the claim is rejected when the accused lack supporting possession evidence and the record supports the other party’s possession.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly cannot be held liable for murder through the assembly’s common object when that object was to cause grievous hurt and the fatal injury was neither shown to be within that object nor known to be likely in its prosecution.
material_facts: The deceased suffered several injuries, including one injury that was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The evidence did not establish which appellant inflicted the fatal injury, and none of the appellants had been specifically charged with causing that injury as murder.
The circumstances showed that the assembly’s common object was to cause grievous hurt with dangerous weapons.
The Court was not satisfied that the fatal injury was inflicted in prosecution of that common object or that the members knew it was likely to be inflicted in its prosecution.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for murder with the aid of the unlawful-assembly rule were set aside, and the appellants were instead convicted of causing grievous hurt with dangerous weapons with the aid of that rule.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code attributes an offence to members of an unlawful assembly when it is committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object or is an offence the members knew to be likely in prosecution of that object. On the facts, the common object was to cause grievous hurt with dangerous weapons, an offence under section 326; the conditions for murder liability under sections 302 and 149 were not established. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_case and fatal_injury_sufficient_to_cause_death and common_object_limited_to_grievous_hurt and fatal_injury_not_within_object and members_lacked_likelihood_knowledge

predicates.unlawful_assembly_case: The prosecution alleges that the accused acted as members of an unlawful assembly.
predicates.fatal_injury_sufficient_to_cause_death: A member of the group inflicted an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
predicates.common_object_limited_to_grievous_hurt: The assembly’s common object was to cause grievous hurt rather than to cause death.
predicates.fatal_injury_not_within_object: The fatal injury was not shown to have been inflicted in prosecution of the assembly’s common object.
predicates.members_lacked_likelihood_knowledge: The evidence did not establish that the members knew the fatal injury was likely to be inflicted in prosecution of the common object.

issues.definition: When an unlawful assembly’s object was limited to causing grievous hurt, and its members neither pursued nor knew that a fatal injury was likely, they are liable for grievous hurt rather than murder.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be convicted for grievous injuries inflicted on an injured victim when the evidence establishes their participation in the group assault.
material_facts: The injured eyewitness sustained ten injuries, including a fracture and other injuries caused by blunt weapons.
The Court found that she was present during the assault and accepted the eyewitness evidence against the appellants.
The High Court had convicted the appellants for the injuries caused to her with the aid of the unlawful-assembly rule.
issues.conclusion: The convictions and sentences for causing grievous hurt to the injured eyewitness with the aid of the unlawful-assembly rule were confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code provides for liability of members of an unlawful assembly for offences committed in prosecution of its common object or known to be likely in its prosecution. The Court confirmed the convictions for grievous hurt to the injured eyewitness on the accepted evidence of the group assault and her injuries. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_case: The prosecution alleges that the accused acted as members of an unlawful assembly.
predicates.injured_victim_sustained_grievous_hurt: A victim of the group assault sustained injuries amounting to grievous hurt.
predicates.accused_participated_in_group_assault: The evidence establishes that the accused participated in the group assault.

issues.definition: When members of an unlawful assembly participated in an assault that caused grievous hurt to a victim, they are convicted for that grievous hurt.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for rioting is sustainable when the evidence establishes that the accused participated in a violent group attack while armed.
material_facts: The accepted evidence established that the appellants participated in the group attack.
The prosecution evidence described the appellants as carrying weapons during the occurrence.
issues.conclusion: The appellants’ convictions for rioting while armed were confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 148 of the Indian Penal Code concerns rioting while armed with a deadly weapon or with an instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death. The Court confirmed the conviction on the accepted evidence of the armed group attack. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_assault_case: The case concerns a criminal assault by a group.
predicates.accused_participated_in_violent_group_at: The evidence establishes that the accused took part in a violent group attack.
predicates.accused_were_armed: The accused carried weapons during the group attack.

issues.definition: When accused persons participated in a violent group attack while armed, their armed-rioting conviction is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for causing hurt to an alleged victim cannot stand when the prosecution has not established that the victim was present and injured in the occurrence.
material_facts: The first report did not mention that the alleged victim was present or injured.
The alleged victim’s presence and injuries were introduced in a police account that the Court found unreliable.
The Court found that the prosecution had not established the alleged victim’s presence.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for causing hurt to the alleged victim and the sentence imposed for that offence were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish the factual basis for the offence, including the alleged victim’s presence and injury. The Court found that the evidence did not establish those facts and rejected the police-introduced account. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_acquittal: The accused challenged a conviction entered after an acquittal in a criminal appeal.
predicates.hurt_conviction_depends_on_victim_presen: The challenged conviction rests on an allegation that a particular victim was present and injured in the occurrence.
predicates.victim_presence_not_established: The prosecution evidence does not establish that the alleged victim was present during the occurrence.

issues.definition: When a hurt conviction depends on a victim’s presence and the prosecution has not established that presence, the conviction for that victim’s injury is set aside.
